%% ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
%% B6 — Multimodal vs Single-Modality Baselines
%% ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

\subsection{Multimodal Fusion Outperforms Single-Modality Baselines}
\label{sec:baselines}

Within the DyAM framework, models restricted to a single data source
achieved repeated-seed (5~seeds~$\times$~10-fold) AUC values of
$0.616 \pm 0.001$ (TMB), $0.635 \pm 0.021$ (pathology IHC-A),
$0.672 \pm 0.021$ (CT radiomics), $0.676 \pm 0.013$ (genomics), and
$0.720 \pm 0.012$ (PD-L1~TPS) on the discovery cohort.
PD-L1~TPS was the strongest individual predictor, consistent with its role
as the biomarker in routine clinical use.

Fusing four data sources (CT radiomics, pathology IHC-G, genomics, and
PD-L1~TPS) under the same protocol raised the AUC to $0.763 \pm 0.022$,
exceeding the best single source by $0.043$~AUC; adding NLP-encoded clinical
variables raised it further to $0.786 \pm 0.017$
(Table~\ref{tab:ovo_all21}).
Multimodal fusion is therefore the primary driver of predictive performance
in this cohort, with no individual source approaching the discrimination of
the fused model.

%% B7 — OvO Attention Comparison
%% ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

\subsection{OvO Competitive Attention Is Comparable to, and in Many-Source Configurations Slightly Higher Than, Cooperative Attention with a Simpler Parameterization}
\label{sec:ovo}

We compared the OvO attention variant with the original cooperative attention across the 21 modality
combinations of the primary paper-matched configuration set (Section~\ref{sec:baselines}),
without and with the NLP-clinical encoding of Section~\ref{sec:nlp_auc}, under the repeated-seed protocol
(5~independent random partitions, 5~seeds~$\times$~10-fold, patient labels re-shuffled per seed;
Table~\ref{tab:ovo_all21}).
Because a cohort of 247 patients cannot support reliable hypothesis tests of differences of this size,
we report the difference in mean AUC and the number of seeds favouring each model, and, where patient-level
scores were retained, bootstrap intervals; we do not use significance testing to claim superiority.

At the primary benchmark (Rad+IHC-G+Gen+PDL1, BM1), OvO reached a repeated-seed mean AUC of $0.771 \pm 0.021$
versus $0.763 \pm 0.022$ for the cooperative model ($\Delta\text{AUC} = +0.008$; OvO higher in four of the five seeds).
The largest gains of OvO over the cooperative model were at TMB+PDL1 ($+0.045$, $0.709$ against $0.664$),
Rad+IHC-A+MutAmp ($+0.021$), Rad+IHC-A+Gen+PDL1 ($+0.019$, $0.755$ against $0.736$), Rad+IHC-A+Gen+TMB+PDL1 ($+0.019$),
Rad+IHC-A+Gen+PDL1+Labs ($+0.017$) and PDL1+Gen ($+0.011$), each in all five seeds; the cooperative model was
higher at IHC-G+Gen ($-0.028$) and by smaller margins in radiomics-only and Rad+IHC-A ($-0.009$ and $-0.007$).

Adding the NLP-clinical encoding in place of the numeric labs raised the AUC in both configurations that contain labs, for both
attention mechanisms: from $0.762$ to $0.786$ for DyAM and from $0.766$ to $0.785$ for OvO at BM2, and from $0.731$ to $0.745$ and from
$0.747$ to $0.769$ in the configuration with IHC-A (Table~\ref{tab:ovo_all21}).
Relative to BM1, which has the same sources without any clinical variable, the NLP gain was $+0.023$ for DyAM
($0.763 \pm 0.022$ to $0.786 \pm 0.017$) and $+0.014$ for OvO ($0.771 \pm 0.021$ to $0.785 \pm 0.022$).
The highest repeated-seed mean AUCs in Table~\ref{tab:ovo_all21} were $0.786$ (DyAM+NLP) and $0.785$ (OvO+NLP) at BM2,
against $0.771$ (OvO) and $0.763$ (DyAM) at BM1.

To examine the NLP-containing models beyond the two configurations with labs, we compared DyAM+NLP and OvO+NLP with the NLP
encoding added as a further source to the six configurations with $k \geq 5$ (Table~\ref{tab:ovo_nlp20}).
OvO+NLP had the higher AUC in all five seeds at Rad+IHC-A+Gen ($+0.010$), Rad+IHC-A+MutAmp ($+0.026$), Rad+IHC-A+Gen+PDL1 ($+0.024$) and
Rad+IHC-A+Gen+TMB+PDL1 ($+0.028$); DyAM+NLP was nominally higher at Rad+IHC-G+Gen ($-0.004$) and at BM1 ($-0.001$).
At BM1 the two ensemble AUCs were $0.799$ (DyAM+NLP) and $0.792$ (OvO+NLP); the patient-level bootstrap intervals of the ensemble differences
were wide and, except for two configurations whose lower bound was close to zero, included zero.

OvO's potential advantage is plausibly one of parameter economy: with the 384-dimensional
NLP source added to BM1, the cooperative model has 4{,}969 trainable parameters against 1{,}242
for OvO, and the advantage of the simpler model was largest at the largest source counts.
We did not test this explanation directly; for example, we did not shrink the cooperative
attention matrix to see whether the gap closes.
Table~\ref{tab:ovo_all21} gives the repeated-seed AUC of both attention mechanisms, with and without NLP, across all 21
configurations, and Table~\ref{tab:ovo_nlp20} the comparison of the NLP-containing models in the six configurations with $k \geq 5$.

%% B8 — NLP AUC Analysis
%% ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

\subsection{NLP Encoding Improves AUC over Numeric Clinical Labs}
\label{sec:nlp_auc}

Seven clinical-encoding variants were evaluated under the DyAM architecture in two pathology
arms (IHC-A: seven variants; IHC-G: four variants), 5~seeds~$\times$~10-fold
(Tables~\ref{tab:auc_ihca} and \ref{tab:auc_ihcg}; Figure~\ref{fig:auc_comparison}).
Relative to numeric labs, the NLP raw (384-dimensional) encoding raised the mean AUC by
$+0.017$ in the IHC-A arm ($0.749$ vs.\ $0.732$) and by $+0.020$ in the IHC-G arm
($0.772$ vs.\ $0.753$); the PCA-compressed NLP variant gave $+0.013$ and $+0.015$.
These differences are of the same order as the partition-to-partition standard deviation
($0.012$--$0.025$), so they should be read as a consistent direction of modest size.
The same advantage over numeric labs was present in the 21-configuration analysis for both
attention mechanisms: in the two seven-source configurations that contain labs
(Table~\ref{tab:ovo_all21}, rows 20 and 21), replacing labs by the NLP encoding raised the
mean AUC from $0.731$ to $0.745$ and from $0.762$ to $0.786$ for DyAM, and from $0.747$ to
$0.769$ and from $0.766$ to $0.785$ for OvO.

\emph{Comparison with no clinical information.}
The comparison with the no-clinical baseline was smaller than the comparison with labs.
In the arm analysis above, the NLP raw encoding was above the no-clinical baseline by $+0.007$ in both arms
(IHC-A: $0.749$ vs.\ $0.741$; IHC-G: $0.772$ vs.\ $0.765$), whereas numeric labs were below it
($-0.010$ and $-0.013$).
At the primary benchmark of the 21-configuration analysis, NLP was above the configuration without clinical
variables by $+0.023$ for DyAM and $+0.014$ for OvO.
The direction therefore agreed between the two analyses, but the size of the gain over omitting clinical
variables ($+0.007$ to $+0.023$) is of the same order as the partition-to-partition spread, so we base the
main claim on NLP versus numeric labs and regard the benefit of NLP encoding over omitting clinical variables
as small and not established in this cohort.

\emph{Domain-specific versus general-purpose encoder.}
Bio\_ClinicalBERT \cite{Alsentzer2019}, PCA-compressed to 16 dimensions,
reached $0.732 \pm 0.012$ in the IHC-A arm, below MiniLM-L6-v2 with the same compression
($0.744 \pm 0.012$; $\Delta\text{AUC} = -0.012$, lower in all five partitions) and below the
no-clinical baseline ($0.741$; Supplementary Note~S2),
consistent with its pretraining objective of masked language modelling
on clinical notes rather than semantic sentence similarity.

\emph{Combined encoding.}
Concatenating numeric labs and the NLP encoding as separate sources
(8 sources in total) did not improve on the NLP encoding alone
(IHC-A: $0.744$ for NLP-PCA16 alone vs.\ $0.736$ for labs + NLP-PCA16),
and with $n/N = 247/8 \approx 31$ the attention weights are poorly determined.
NLP encoding is therefore used as a \emph{replacement} for,
rather than an addition to, numeric clinical features.

%% B9 — Survival Analysis
%% ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

\subsection{Survival Analysis: Clinical Encoding Raises the Hazard Ratio of the Risk Score}
\label{sec:survival}

Under 5~seeds~$\times$~10-fold evaluation, the DyAM risk score was strongly associated with
progression-free survival in multivariate Cox regression adjusted for age, ECOG
performance status, serum albumin, dNLR, and liver metastasis status, in every model
variant (hazard ratio per unit of risk score 4.0--4.6; Table~\ref{tab:survival}).

\paragraph{Cox hazard ratios.}
In both arms the hazard ratio was higher with the NLP encodings than without a clinical encoding:
IHC-A, $4.12$ (no clinical) vs.\ $4.13$ (labs), $4.52$ (NLP raw) and $4.43$ (NLP-PCA16);
IHC-G, $4.02$ vs.\ $4.54$, $4.63$ and $4.47$.
Numeric labs raised the hazard ratio in the IHC-G arm only.
The NLP encodings gave the numerically highest hazard ratios (by about 0.1 over labs in IHC-G and 0.4 in IHC-A),
but these differences are of the same order as the partition-to-partition spread
($0.2$--$0.6$), so the data do not reliably distinguish NLP from numeric labs on this endpoint.

\paragraph{C-index.}
Harrell's C-index was $0.61$--$0.62$ for all variants and differed by at most $0.006$
between encodings in either arm; numeric labs gave the highest value in both arms
(IHC-A: $0.614$ vs.\ $0.609$ for NLP raw; IHC-G: $0.623$ vs.\ $0.617$), and the NLP variants did not exceed the no-clinical
baseline in the IHC-A arm ($0.608$--$0.609$ vs.\ $0.608$).

\paragraph{Kaplan--Meier stratification.}
Dichotomising patients at the median risk score gave a log-rank $\chi^2$ above 3.84
($p < 0.05$) in all 55 model--partition combinations (smallest value 7.0) and above 7.88
($p < 0.005$) in 53 of them (Table~\ref{tab:km}).
The mean log-rank $\chi^2$ was higher with clinical encodings than without
(IHC-A: $16.9$ without vs.\ $19.5$ with labs and $19.3$ with NLP raw; IHC-G: $13.6$ vs.\ $14.5$
and $15.3$), again with no consistent separation between NLP and labs.
Kaplan--Meier curves of the primary benchmark models are shown in
Figure~\ref{fig:km_curves}, and the five-partition summary of survival metrics in
Figure~\ref{fig:survival_summary}.
Time-dependent AUC (Table~\ref{tab:survival}) was $0.63$--$0.69$ at 6, 12 and 18~months for every variant
and differed by about $0.03$ or less between encodings within an arm; it was not systematically higher with the
NLP encodings (IHC-A at 12~months: $0.689$ with NLP raw, $0.684$ with labs, $0.684$ without clinical
variables; at 18~months the no-clinical variants were the highest, $0.662$ and $0.655$).

\paragraph{OvO attention with the NLP encoding at the primary benchmark.}
We also compared the survival association of the four attention/encoding models at the primary benchmark
(Rad+IHC-G+Gen+PDL1; 5~seeds~$\times$~10-fold, risk scores standardised, hazard ratio per
1~s.d.\ adjusted for the same covariates).
The hazard ratio rose from $1.53$ for cooperative attention (DyAM) to $1.58$ for OvO, $1.60$ for DyAM with NLP and
$1.64$ for OvO with NLP (log hazard ratio $0.425$, $0.460$, $0.468$ and $0.495$); the log-rank $\chi^2$ rose from $12.3$
to $14.4$, $16.3$ and $17.9$, and the C-index from $0.616$ to $0.620$, $0.622$ and $0.623$.
Relative to DyAM, OvO with NLP had a higher log hazard ratio in all 5 seeds ($+0.070$ on average; $95\%$ patient-bootstrap
interval $0.013$ to $0.106$) and a higher C-index in all 5 seeds ($+0.006$), the latter within the bootstrap interval of zero.
OvO with NLP was higher than DyAM with NLP by $+0.027$ in log hazard ratio (5 of 5 seeds) and by $+0.001$ in C-index, and the two
risk scores were highly correlated ($r = 0.99$), so the gain relative to DyAM came from the OvO mechanism and the NLP encoding
together, about $+0.035$ and $+0.043$ each when added alone.
The same ordering was obtained in two other software environments (Windows, scikit-learn 1.1.1 and 0.24.2; log hazard ratio
difference to DyAM $+0.070$ and $+0.076$).

\paragraph{Survival association across the 21 configurations.}
We repeated this evaluation on all 21 configurations of Table~\ref{tab:ovo_all21} (5~seeds~$\times$~10-fold; Tables~\ref{tab:surv21} and \ref{tab:surv21b}).
The association of the risk score with survival grew with the number of fused sources: for the single-source scores
the C-index was $0.567$--$0.587$ and the 12-month time-dependent AUC $0.596$--$0.661$, whereas for the configurations with five to
seven sources (14--21) the C-index was $0.588$--$0.627$, the 12-month time-dependent AUC $0.657$--$0.709$ and the log hazard ratio per
1~s.d.\ $0.362$--$0.505$.
In each of these eight configurations the mean log hazard ratio, 12-month time-dependent AUC and C-index of OvO were above those of cooperative attention
(for example, at BM1 the log hazard ratio $0.460$ against $0.425$ and the 12-month time-dependent AUC $0.709$ against $0.681$; the C-index differences were
between $+0.001$ and $+0.016$).
In the two configurations that contain labs, OvO with the NLP encoding had the highest log hazard ratio ($0.495$ at BM2 and $0.497$ in configuration~20,
against $0.416$ and $0.411$ for DyAM, and $0.468$ and $0.450$ for DyAM with NLP; higher than DyAM in all 5 seeds in both configurations),
and the highest 12-month time-dependent AUC ($0.708$ and $0.704$, against $0.675$ and $0.678$ for DyAM), with a C-index within $0.01$ of DyAM
($0.623$ against $0.626$ at BM2; $0.617$ against $0.613$ in configuration~20).
The Kaplan--Meier log-rank statistic (mean over the 5 seeds) showed the same direction: OvO was above cooperative attention in the six configurations with five to seven sources that do not contain labs (14--19; for example $14.4$ against $12.3$ at BM1 and $19.9$ against $12.1$ in configuration~19), and at BM2 ($17.6$ against $15.2$; $17.9$ for OvO with NLP), whereas in configuration~20 the cooperative model was higher ($20.5$ against $14.3$; $17.6$ for OvO with NLP).
For several configurations with fewer sources the two mechanisms were close or OvO was lower (for example TMB+PDL1 and IHC-G+Gen).
